clue.text: The person in charge is a knob

definitions.meaning: first meaning: the one who gives the orders at work
second meaning: a raised stud or round ornament on a surface, as on a shield

explanation.walkthrough: The surface reads as an insult aimed at a manager, with 'knob' as British slang for an idiot; the word is really the decorative stud.
explanation.definitionFit: The word names both an employer or manager and a rounded projecting stud, two unrelated senses of one spelling.

clue.text: Cause excessive strain to old, old monarch: that's clear all round

indicators.note: the word for clear surrounds the other letters

parts.note: overt means plain, openly visible
ex means former
ER, Elizabeth Regina, the late Queen

explanation.surface: An elderly king is being worn out by a too-demanding task.
explanation.walkthrough: ER, for Elizabeth Regina, is the crossword's Queen; since 2022 she is a former monarch.
explanation.definitionFit: To push oneself or something too hard is to strain it beyond a sensible limit.

clue.text: Small business held up by No 10? It's a sign

indicators.note: in a down entry, the earlier pieces sit on top of the letters for ten

parts.note: corp is short for corporation, a business
the figure 10 looks like the letters I and O

explanation.surface: A small firm is delayed by Downing Street, which someone takes as an omen.
explanation.walkthrough: No 10 suggests 10 Downing Street, the Prime Minister's home; here it is just the digits, read as letters.
explanation.definitionFit: Scorpio, the scorpion, is one of the twelve zodiac signs of astrology.

clue.text: A system? Not at home

parts.note: a way of doing something is a method or system

explanation.surface: A puzzled question about some scheme, answered by someone who is out.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone who is absent from their house is said to be elsewhere, the adverb used of people out or travelling.

clue.text: Australian, a little tease, to prove alluring — or try

indicators.note: just a small piece of the word: its first letter

parts.note: the first letter of tease
to tempt is to be enticing

explanation.surface: An Australian is weighing whether to flirt a bit or simply have a go.
explanation.definitionFit: An attempt is an effort or go at something, so the verb means to have a go.

clue.text: Dined at home from single can, reportedly

indicators.note: as it is said aloud, so the phrase built here sounds like the answer

parts.note: a single can is a tin, said as 'a tin'

explanation.surface: Someone had their supper indoors straight out of one can.
explanation.definitionFit: To have eaten in is to have taken a meal at home rather than at a restaurant.

clue.text: Pretty vacant, taken in by hoax surveillance kit

indicators.note: the letters are held inside the hoax, as a dupe is taken in by one

parts.note: a scam is a hoax or swindle

indicators.note: emptied of its contents, leaving only the outer letters

parts.note: the first and last letters of pretty

explanation.surface: A rather empty-headed person is fooled by a con involving spy gadgets.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Pretty vacant' reads as 'rather empty' (also a Sex Pistols song) but supplies the outer letters.
explanation.definitionFit: A hidden camera used to watch people covertly is a piece of spying equipment.

clue.text: Islands separated? These hairlines might interlink, primarily!

definitions.text: Islands separated? These hairlines might interlink, primarily!

indicators.note: in the first place, so only the opening letter of each word is taken

parts.words: Islands separated? These hairlines might interlink
parts.note: the initial letters of these six words

explanation.surface: A geographer suggests that thin strips of land could join islands that lie apart.
explanation.walkthrough: The whole clue does both jobs: its initials spell the answer and it describes narrow necks of land joining two masses.
explanation.definitionFit: An isthmus is a narrow strip of land linking two larger areas; the clue's hairlines are such strips.

clue.text: In Athens, fat people edited film

indicators.note: edited text has been cut and rearranged, so the letters of the three words are put in a new order

explanation.surface: Some overweight Greeks have been cut out of a movie in post-production.
explanation.walkthrough: 'edited' sits naturally with 'film', which hides that it works on the words before it.
explanation.definitionFit: This is the 1968 science-fiction movie about astronauts on a world ruled by apes, remade several times.

clue.text: Terrible mess, perhaps, setter's table

definitions.meaning: first meaning: a British idiom for a botched muddle
second meaning: what a setter (a breed of gun dog) eats, its board or fare

explanation.walkthrough: 'setter' looks like the puzzle's author; it is the dog. 'perhaps' marks a setter as one example of a dog.
explanation.definitionFit: The British idiom means a shambles; literally it is a hound's meal, and 'table' can mean the food served.

clue.text: Business bending paper-thin, vacuous regulations

indicators.note: bent out of shape, so the letters are rearranged
empty, so only the outer letters of the word remain

parts.note: the first and last letters of regulations

explanation.surface: A firm flexes rules that were already flimsy and empty of meaning.
explanation.definitionFit: A partnership is a firm owned jointly by two or more people sharing its profits.

clue.text: Detailed photo? Stop talking!

definitions.meaning: first meaning: a picture taken from very near the subject

explanation.walkthrough: As a noun it is a camera shot; as a verb phrase it is a curt order to be quiet.
explanation.definitionFit: A tight camera shot shows fine detail, while to close up also means to fall silent or clam up.

clue.text: Pharaoh perhaps included in symposium on archaeology

indicators.note: the letters are contained within the run of words that follows, spanning their boundaries

parts.note: the letters run across the end of symposium, all of on and the start of archaeology

explanation.surface: An Egyptian ruler is the subject of a talk at an academic conference on digs.
explanation.definitionFit: A pharaoh was a king of ancient Egypt, an example of a sovereign ruler, hence the 'perhaps'.

clue.text: Inaccurately describe importers' bananas

indicators.note: bananas is slang for crazy, so the letters of the word before go wild into a new order

explanation.surface: Someone gets the facts wrong about fruit that traders have shipped in.
explanation.walkthrough: 'bananas' looks like the importers' cargo, but it is the slang word for mad.
explanation.definitionFit: To give a false or inaccurate account of events is to misrepresent them in a report.

clue.text: Regressive 'topless' wordplay, not entirely new: Everyman prompting weariness

indicators.note: going backwards, so the combined letters of the bracketed pieces are read in reverse
without its top, so the opening letter of the word for wordplay is lost

parts.note: a pun is a piece of wordplay

indicators.note: only part of the word is used, so its final letter is dropped

parts.note: the setter refers to themself, giving the pronoun I

explanation.surface: The setter confesses that their stale, half-recycled punning is wearing solvers out.
explanation.walkthrough: A setter's name in a clue stands for I or ME, as the setter speaking.
explanation.definitionFit: This French borrowing means listless boredom, a jaded tiredness with everything.

clue.text: What remains of razed supermarket, you say: a few small hairs

indicators.note: spoken aloud, the phrase sounds like the answer

parts.note: after a shop burns down, its aisle is left as ashes: aisle ashes

explanation.surface: Someone asks what's left of a demolished store, and gets a handful of hairs as the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: The hairs fringing the eyelids are a set of short, fine hairs.

clue.text: C17-18 satirist who penned Shake It Off

definitions.meaning: first meaning: Jonathan ... (1667-1745), author of Gulliver's Travels
second meaning: Taylor ..., who wrote and sang the 2014 hit

explanation.walkthrough: The clue reads as one writer, but two people share the surname: an Anglo-Irish satirist and an American pop star.
explanation.definitionFit: Jonathan the satirical author and Taylor the songwriter share this family name.

clue.text: Very rainy — I'm surprised — somewhere in S Africa

parts.note: so means very, as in so cold
wet weather is rainy
O is an exclamation of surprise

explanation.surface: A visitor exclaims at the downpour somewhere in South Africa.
explanation.definitionFit: Soweto is a large township next to Johannesburg, famous for the 1976 student uprising.

clue.text: Underarm's faltering: beat this!

indicators.note: stumbling and unsteady, so the letters of the word before are jumbled

explanation.surface: An underarm throw is wobbling, and someone challenges another to do better.
explanation.walkthrough: 'beat this!' sounds like a boast; read literally, it describes an instrument that is struck.
explanation.definitionFit: A drummer strikes this percussion instrument with sticks; it has a rattle of wires across its lower head.

clue.text: Ex-president, leader of Zimbabwe okays reforms adopting rand

indicators.note: taking in, so the letter for rand goes inside
reshapes, so these letters are put in a new order
the leader is the first letter

parts.note: the first letter of Zimbabwe
R is the symbol of the South African rand

explanation.surface: Zimbabwe's head approves economic changes including adopting the South African currency.
explanation.walkthrough: The rand is South Africa's currency, abbreviated R.
explanation.definitionFit: Nicolas Sarkozy was President of France from 2007 to 2012, so a former head of state.

clue.text: American made American biopic

parts.note: US, the United States

explanation.surface: A film about someone's life was produced in the States.
explanation.definitionFit: Amadeus is the 1984 film about Mozart's life, as seen by his rival Salieri.

clue.text: American backing school for doctors, one wanting decapitation

indicators.note: supporting from behind, so the American letters follow the school

parts.note: med school is where doctors train
USA, the United States of America

explanation.surface: An American sponsor of a medical school wants someone's head cut off.
explanation.walkthrough: 'backing' tempts a reversal, but here it only places one piece behind the other.
explanation.definitionFit: Medusa, the Gorgon whose gaze turned people to stone, was beheaded by Perseus in Greek myth.

clue.text: Party to unwind, so Rolfing a kind of knot

indicators.note: being party to something is sharing in it, so the answer is part of the words that follow

parts.note: the letters run from inside unwind, through so, into the start of Rolfing

explanation.surface: A tie knot is mentioned amid talk of relaxing with Rolfing, a deep-tissue massage therapy.
explanation.definitionFit: The Windsor is a wide, symmetrical way of tying a necktie, named after the Duke of Windsor.

clue.text: Channel, one doing some embroidery

definitions.meaning: first meaning: a drain or underground conduit for waste
second meaning: one who sews, pronounced differently

explanation.walkthrough: One spelling, two pronunciations: a drain and a person stitching.
explanation.definitionFit: A sewer is a pipe carrying waste water, and also a person who stitches with needle and thread.

clue.text: After a party, journalist shamefaced

indicators.note: the journalist's letters come after those for a party

parts.note: a bash is an informal party
ED, short for editor, the crossword's stock journalist

explanation.surface: A reporter feels embarrassed the morning after a celebration.
explanation.definitionFit: Being embarrassed and ashamed of oneself is the same feeling as being disconcerted or sheepish.

clue.text: Dance, and unsettle sundry squares?

parts.note: to throw someone is to unsettle or disconcert them
sundry means various, some
squares are examples of shapes

explanation.surface: Someone dances wildly, and the question asks if that disturbs a few town squares.
explanation.walkthrough: To throw some shapes is British slang for dancing flamboyantly; the question mark flags that the squares are only examples of shapes.
explanation.definitionFit: The British slang phrase means to dance energetically, striking poses and moves on a dance floor.

clue.text: Goods cart, just under 1m in length, rejected

indicators.note: sent back, so the letters of the length are read in reverse

parts.note: a yard is 0.914 metres, just short of a metre

explanation.surface: A goods wagon a little shorter than a metre is turned away.
explanation.definitionFit: A dray is a low, heavy cart without sides, traditionally used by brewers for barrels.

clue.text: Ornamental band showing RIP — LEFT — DEPARTED

indicators.note: having gone away, so the letter for left is taken out of the tear

parts.note: a slash is a rip or tear, as in a slashed tyre

explanation.surface: A decorative band bears words like a mourning ribbon or a tombstone: rest in peace, gone.
explanation.walkthrough: RIP looks like 'rest in peace', but it is a tear; L is the usual abbreviation for left.
explanation.definitionFit: A sash is a broad strip of cloth worn over the shoulder or round the waist as decoration or insignia.
